questions.q: Define "forest cover" as per Forest Survey of India and state the minimum canopy density threshold for "Very Dense Forest", "Moderately Dense Forest", and "Open Forest" categories.
questions.a: Forest cover (FSI) = all lands >1 ha with tree canopy density >10%, irrespective of ownership/legal status. Very Dense Forest (VDF) ≥70% canopy density; Moderately Dense Forest (MDF) 40-70%; Open Forest (OF) 10-40%. A wrong answer (e.g., using 30% for VDF or confusing "forest area" legal classification with "forest cover" remote sensing classification) reveals confusion between administrative categories (Reserved/Protected/Unclassed forests) and biophysical assessment — a frequent board exam error.

questions.q: Explain why the "forest transition theory" (forest cover stabilizes then increases with economic development) does NOT automatically apply to India's Northeastern states despite rising per capita income.
questions.a: Northeastern states (Arunachal, Manipur, Nagaland, Mizoram) show persistent forest cover decline (ISFR 2021: -1,020 km² since 2019) due to: (1) shifting cultivation (jhum) shortening fallow cycles from 15-20 to 3-5 years under population pressure, (2) conversion to monoculture plantations (oil palm, rubber) counted as "forest cover" but not biodiversity-rich forest, (3) infrastructure projects (roads, dams) in sensitive hill ecosystems, and (4) weak enforcement of Forest Conservation Act 1980 due to special constitutional provisions (Article 371A/G). A student citing only "economic development leads to reforestation" misses the institutional and cultural context — a classic competitive exam trap.

questions.q: Using the species-area relationship S = cA^z (where S = species richness, A = habitat area, c = constant, z ≈ 0.25 for forest fragments), calculate the expected percentage of bird species lost if a 10,000 km² contiguous forest in the Western Ghats is fragmented into 25 isolated patches of 400 km² each. Assume no migration between patches.
questions.a: Step 1: Original species richness S₁ = c(10,000)^0.25 = c × 10. Step 2: Species per fragment S₂ = c(400)^0.25 = c × 4.47. Step 3: Total species across 25 isolated fragments = 25 × c × 4.47 = 111.75c (but this overcounts shared species; with zero migration, each fragment loses unique species). Step 4: Realistic estimate uses z=0.25 for each fragment: S₂/S₁ = (400/10,000)^0.25 = (0.04)^0.25 = 0.447. Each fragment retains ~44.7% of original species pool. Step 5: With no migration, gamma diversity (landscape-level) drops to ~44.7% of original → **55.3% species loss**. A wrong answer (e.g., 25 × 44.7% = 1117%) shows misunderstanding of alpha vs gamma diversity and the non-additivity of species across isolated fragments.

questions.q: Compare the drivers of deforestation in Central India's tropical dry deciduous forests (Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh) with those in the Western Ghats' tropical evergreen forests (Karnataka, Kerala). Identify two similarities and two differences in the underlying socio-economic forces.
questions.a: Similarities: (1) Agricultural expansion — both regions face conversion to cropland (soybean/cotton in Central India; coffee/tea/arecanut in Ghats). (2) Infrastructure-driven fragmentation — linear projects (roads, railways, power lines) dissect forests in both. Differences: (1) Central India: mining (coal, iron ore, bauxite) is the dominant driver due to mineral-rich Gondwana basins; Western Ghats: plantation agriculture and tourism infrastructure dominate due to high rainfall and market access. (2) Central India: high dependence on fuelwood and NTFP by tribal communities (collection pressure); Western Ghats: higher commercial plantation pressure from corporate/private estates. A student listing only "agriculture" for both misses the mineral vs plantation distinction critical for region-specific policy.

questions.q: Critique the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act (CAMPA) 2016 as a tool for mitigating biodiversity loss from forest diversion. Use three criteria: ecological equivalence, temporal lag, and social justice.
questions.a: Ecological equivalence: FAILS — CAMPA funds monoculture plantations (teak, eucalyptus, acacia) on non-forest land (often revenue wastelands) which cannot replace complex native forest structure, endemic species, or soil microbiome. Temporal lag: FAILS — a 50-year-old forest diverted today takes 50+ years to regain equivalent carbon/biodiversity; CAMPA does not require "advance" afforestation. Social justice: FAILS — plantations often displace forest-dwelling communities from traditional use areas; Gram Sabha consent under Forest Rights Act 2006 is frequently bypassed. A student saying "CAMPA plants trees so it compensates" confuses tree cover with forest ecosystem — a fundamental category error in environmental governance.

questions.q: Design a landscape-level conservation plan for a 5,000 km² region in the Central Indian tiger corridor (Kanha-Pench) that balances tiger connectivity, tribal livelihoods (NTFP, agriculture), and climate resilience. Specify: (a) core protection zones, (b) corridor design principles, (c) community-based incentives, and (d) monitoring metrics.
questions.a: (a) Core zones: Existing PAs (Kanha, Pench, Phen, Narnawapuram) + identified Critical Tiger Habitats = ~2,500 km² under strict protection (no extraction). (b) Corridors: 3-5 km wide multi-use corridors along Pench, Wainganga, and Maikal hill ranges using least-cost path modeling (resistance surface: forest cover, human density, road density); corridors include Community Forest Resource (CFR) areas under FRA 2006. (c) Incentives: (i) Payment for Ecosystem Services (PES) for corridor maintenance by Gram Sabhas, (ii) NTFP value-chain support (mahua, tendu, honey) with MSP guarantee, (iii) Climate-smart agriculture (millets, agroforestry) in buffer villages. (d) Metrics: Tiger occupancy (camera traps), corridor functionality (genetic flow via scat DNA), forest cover change (annual LISS-IV), household income from NTFP/agroforestry, and human-wildlife conflict incidents. A poor answer proposes only "more national parks" ignoring the corridor-matrix-human dimension — a narrow preservationist view that fails in democratic landscapes.
